title: Remember, and find peace
hookLine: simro simar simar sukh paavo: remember, remember, and find peace (Sukhmani 1)
last: I BOW — FOUR BOWS TO THE GURU.

lines: A NAME, A STORY, A PHOTO.
cards: How do you remember a phone number someone just told you? You say it again. And again, under your breath, all the way to the pen.
How do you remember a person who has died? You say their name, tell their stories, keep their photo where you'll see it.

A lot of remembering is repetition: not one grand act, but something done again and again until it becomes part of you. That's how the first stanza of Sukhmani begins: with one word, said three times in a row.

teach.b: The first stanza opens: simro simar simar sukh paavo.
I remember, and remembering, remembering, I find peace. Then, in paraphrase: the troubles and anguish of the body are erased. The word under all of it is simran, remembrance.
In Sikh life, simran means remembering God, and in practice it often means repeating the Name, Waheguru, quietly or aloud, again and again. Listen to how the line does what it describes.
Simro, simar, simar: three beats before the reward arrives. Sukh paavo: I find peace. Sukh, the same sukh as in Sukhmani.
So the jewel of peace this bani is named for is found, right at the start, by remembering.

teach.h: THE ONE WORD THE SCRIPTURES CAME FROM.
teach.b: The stanza goes on, in paraphrase: the Vedas, the Puranas and the Simritis, the great scriptures of Guru Arjan's world, were made from the one word of the Name.

The person in whose heart even a tiny particle of it lives has a glory no one can count. Then it closes, as the stanzas will, in Nanak's voice: those who long only for the sight of You, save me with them.
Here's what makes simran different from just thinking about God.
A thought comes once and is finished. Simran is a practice, a phone number said over and over until your mouth knows it before your mind does.
And the stanza promises peace in that repeating.

how: Sikhs practice simran by repeating the Name, Waheguru, quietly or aloud, alone or together in the sangat; some use a mala of beads to count, and some keep the Name going through the day's ordinary tasks.

o: a deep study of the scriptures, line by line
a quiet fast kept on one day each week
remembering God, often by repeating the Name

games.q: you want peace, the jewel the bani is named for. what does the first stanza of Sukhmani say to do?
o: think hard about God, once, deeply.
games.why: simro simar simar sukh paavo: remembering, and remembering again, you find peace.

practice: If you pray, say Waheguru slowly ten times, aloud or in your head, each one riding on an out-breath; if not, choose a word that steadies you, peace, or thank you, or a name you love, and repeat it the same way.
Count on your fingers if it helps, and don't hurry toward ten. When you reach it, sit in the quiet afterward.

wordCard.voice: Simran. Remembering God, often by repeating the Name; Sukhmani's first stanza says that remembering, again and again, brings peace.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: simran, remembrance; the practice Sukhmani opens with.

carryVoice: Your line: remember, find peace. Three beats of remembering, and then the peace. See you tomorrow.
